content: During the months of April to June (dry season) and June to October (monsoon season), one site encountered repeated errors with a GeneXpert machine. These errors were attributed to an unstable electricity supply, including power outages and fluctuating voltage levels. The issue was resolved by installing an online uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system, which stabilized the voltage and provided 1–2 hours of backup electricity to ensure the completion of test cycles. In Yangon, daily temperatures range from an average low of 17°C to a high of 32°C, with peak temperatures reaching 39°C in March and April. Humidity levels vary from an average of 65% during the dry season to 85% in the monsoon season. These environmental conditions posed challenges for the storage of test kits and reagents, as well as for the operation of diagnostic devices. Test kits and reagents require storage at temperatures below 30°C and are susceptible to damage from high humidity. To address this, 91 sites were advised to store test kits and reagents in refrigerators until the day of use. However, the storage of rapid diagnostic test (RDT) kits and GeneXpert cartridges required significant refrigerator space. Standard household refrigerators were procured for this purpose, but laboratory-grade refrigerators may be more suitable for storing test kit reagents and cartridge boxes, as they allow for easier access and better stock monitoring. Cost and suitability should be considered when procuring refrigerators specifically for stock storage. GeneXpert devices require annual maintenance, which includes on-site checks by technical support personnel from the distributor. Additionally, ad hoc maintenance and module replacements are necessary if recurrent errors occur. During the rainy season, both sites experienced recurrent errors over several days, necessitating the installation of online UPS systems and voltage stabilizers to improve power supply reliability and protect the machines. The error rate for the GeneXpert HCV Viral Load assay across the study was 5% of the total tests conducted. Errors were defined as any erroneous output, no result, or invalid result produced during the assay. The study included 1,137 HCV VL assays for diagnosing active HCV infection and assessing sustained virological response at 12 weeks (SVR12). Sites were enrolled in the External Quality Assessment Scheme (EQAS) program for HCV Viral Load testing through the Australian National Serology Reference Laboratory, along with national laboratories in Myanmar. Quarterly test events were conducted, and the sites participated in three of these events. Minimal internal quality control (IQC) was performed at the sites starting midway through the study period. This involved weekly unblinded testing using known positive and negative specimens provided by the National Health Laboratory in Yangon or cross-clinic specimens, which could be stored at 4°C for up to a month. Regular quality assurance checks were conducted to ensure proper use of the GeneXpert device and to identify errors. Troubleshooting of errors and recurrent issues was also performed. External support for sites to conduct IQC and participate in EQAS must be tailored to specific contexts, considering feasibility, affordability, and practicality for government or private laboratories. Training and assistance in preparing and uploading test event results in the required format were provided to sites prior to EQAS enrollment. GeneXpert HCV viral load cartridges have a shelf life of 12 months from the date of manufacture. For this project, the cartridges typically had a shelf life of 6–9 months after clearing customs and arriving at clinics. This required regular supply through local distributors and accurate demand forecasting. Confirmation of undetectable HCV RNA in previously viraemic individuals is critical for assessing virological response to direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment. Before the introduction of curative oral DAA regimens, interferon-based treatments required frequent monitoring of HCV RNA levels during therapy to determine whether treatment should be stopped or shortened. With the advent of DAAs, such frequent assessments are no longer necessary due to their higher efficacy and the infrequency of viral breakthrough. In most individuals treated with DAAs, HCV RNA becomes undetectable within four weeks of treatment initiation. A single negative (undetectable) HCV RNA test at 12 weeks after therapy completion (SVR12) is now the standard for assessing treatment outcomes and cure, using either qualitative or quantitative HCV RNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) assays. The 2017 WHO Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing recommend the use of laboratory-based HCV RNA NAT assays for qualitative or quantitative detection of HCV RNA as a test of cure at 12 or 24 weeks (SVR12 or SVR24) after completing antiviral treatment. Point-of-care (POC) HCV RNA NAT assays with comparable limits of detection (LoD) to laboratory-based assays are also recommended as an alternative approach for testing cure. A multi-cohort analysis of 66,640 individuals at diagnosis established that 97% had HCV RNA levels greater than 1,318 IU/mL, and 95% had levels greater than 3,311 IU/mL. WHO pre-qualified laboratory-based assays have analytical sensitivity as low as 12 IU/mL and 5 IU/mL for qualitative HCV RNA detection by NAT. The LoD for POC HCV RNA assays is 10 IU/mL for GeneXpert using venous blood and 100 IU/mL with fingerstick capillary blood. The GeneDrive instrument has a reported LoD of 2,362 IU/mL, and core antigen assays have an LoD of 1,000–3,000 IU/mL. All assays are acceptable for diagnosing viraemic HCV infection, but further studies are needed to determine whether HCV core antigen and POC HCV RNA assays can also be used to assess sustained virological response and serve as a test of cure. The European Association for the Study of the Liver Diseases and the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases/Infectious Diseases Society of America recommend a minimum LoD of 1,000 IU/mL for HCV diagnosis but do not specify minimal performance characteristics for a test of cure. Based on multi-cohort analysis, HCV RNA assays with an LoD of around 1,000 IU/mL would identify at least 95% of viraemic infections. Technologies capable of detecting viral HCV RNA levels down to 1,000 IU/mL are sufficient for clinical decision-making in most individuals. The Guidelines Development Group recommends the use of POC HCV RNA NAT assays as a test of cure with LoD comparable to laboratory-based assays. However, the data on HCV core antigen assays for treatment monitoring and assessment of cure (SVR) is too limited to recommend their use as a substitute for HCV RNA NAT at SVR12. Increasing the availability of validated POC NAT assays and reducing costs of both qualitative and quantitative NAT will be critical to improving access to diagnosis and monitoring in lowand middle-income countries. Reflex testing, which links HCV RNA (or HCV antigen) testing to an initial positive HCV antibody screening test, may accelerate access to HCV RNA testing. Reflex testing can be implemented in laboratory-based or clinic-based settings, reducing the need for multiple clinical encounters and ensuring prompt confirmation of active viraemic HCV infection.
